ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Mean age was 68.2 ± 9.3 years, mean disease duration was 12.1 ± 6.7 years, and 22 of 23 participants were men.

> Anatomical models reduced squared prediction error by 26.7-35.0% relative to the benchmark, although the advantage diminished substantially after influential participants were excluded.

> This advantage persisted when influential participants were excluded one at a time, suggesting that pathway engagement added predictive information beyond stimulation volume within this cohort.

> All 19 participants had some modeled Field of Forel coverage on at least one side.

> Although the axons recruited by DBS in our participants belonged to neurons that also influence these midbrain regions remains a speculation, the combined coverage measure identifies a region in which engagement of neighboring or overlapping pathways are associated with better gaze holding.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: Mean age was 68.2 ± 9.3 years, mean disease duration was 12.1 ± 6.7 years, and 22 of 23 participants were men.
Anatomical models reduced squared prediction error by 26.7-35.0% relative to the benchmark, although the advantage diminished substantially after influential participants were excluded.
This advantage persisted when influential participants were excluded one at a time, suggesting that pathway engagement added predictive information beyond stimulation volume within this cohort.
All 19 participants had some modeled Field of Forel coverage on at least one side.

Although the axons recruited by DBS in our participants belonged to neurons that also influence these midbrain regions remains a speculation, the combined coverage measure identifies a region in which engagement of neighboring or overlapping pathways are associated with better gaze holding.

text.text: Financial Disclosure and Conflict of Interest: Shaikh serves on speaker bureau for Merz Therapeutics.
Looking up from a distant object and back to a line of print requires the eyes to change their relative angle (vergence) and hold the new alignment while taking in visual information.

In Parkinson's disease (PD), abnormal basal ganglia activity may disrupt this process, directly or indirectly, altering how and when a vergence begins (latency), whether there is a slow smooth vergence or it is associated with rapid saccades (motor strategy), and how steadily the eyes maintain their position after vergence (gaze holding) (Almer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In Parkinson's disease (PD), abnormal basal ganglia activity may disrupt this process, directly or indirectly, altering how and when a vergence begins (latency), whether there is a slow smooth vergence or it is associated with rapid saccades (motor strategy), and how steadily the eyes maintain their position after vergence (gaze holding) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Almer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A shift in viewing depth can occur through vergence alone or in combination with a disconjugate saccade, rapidly reducing vergence error.
Basal ganglia output and subthalamic nucleus (STN) activity may influence when a depth shift begins, whether a saccade is recruited, and when and how much it contributes.
These effects can dissociate.
More frequent saccades may not improve accuracy, and a larger saccadic contribution may leave final vergence gain unchanged (Busettini and Mays, 2005 , Quinet et al., 2020 , Zee et al., 1992).

text.text: Primate physiology identifies several routes for this control.
Neurons in and around the supraoculomotor area (SOA) encode vergence velocity, angle, or both (Mays, 1984 , Mays et al., 1986 , Zhang et al., 1991).

text.text: The STN may influence saccade initiation through the substantia nigra pars reticulata, whose inhibitory output regulates the superior colliculus (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985, Van Horn et al., 2013).

text.text: Collicular projections to the SOA and pontocerebellar circuits involving the nucleus reticularis tegmenti pontis (NRTP) may coordinate saccades with vergence (Bostan et al., 2010 , Gamlin and Clarke, 1995 , Glickstein et al., 1990 , May et al., 2021 , Stanton et al., 1988 , Takeichi et al., 2005).

text.text: Cerebellar fastigial and interposed nuclei project to the superior colliculus, midbrain near-response regions, and central mesencephalic reticular formation (cMRF) (Bohlen et al., 2021 , May et al., 1990 , May et al., 1992).

text.text: In the cMRF, saccadevergence burst neurons encode vergence velocity during disconjugate saccades.
The saccadic contribution to a depth shift depends on the interaction between the burst and the remaining vergence error (Busettini and Mays, 2005, Quinet et al., 2020).

text.text: We hypothesized that stimulation alters vergence latency and saccade recruitment through modulation of frontal-basal ganglia signaling in the associative STN and possible antidromic recruitment of nearby cerebellothalamic fibers.
Altered cerebellar output could change when the saccadic burst arrives relative to the remaining vergence error and how much it contributes to binocular alignment.
Maintaining alignment after a depth shift requires a vergence neural integrator that converts brief velocity commands into sustained position signals.
The velocity and angle signals encoded in and around the SOA make this region a candidate substrate (Mays, 1984 , Mays et al., 1986 , Quinet et al., 2025).

text.text: Connectomic analysis was performed using the HCP 1065 atlas to objectively examine the VTA overlap with number of white-matter tracks, including fields of Forel, cerebellothalamic projections, rubrospinal tracts, and cortico-pontine pathways.
We compared convergence and divergence during DBS on and off in PD participants, retaining paired visits and determining eligibility separately for each outcome and direction.
Outcomes included latency, first, intermediate, and final gain, gaze holding, and movement strategy.
Gain was signed relative to demand, with unity indicating the requested amplitude.
Absolute gain errors were calculated per take as |gain -1| and multiplied by demand to obtain angular errors.
Subsequent correction was initial minus final error.
Measurements were matched within participant, visit, direction, and nominal demand.
Takes were averaged, using medians for latency, followed by equal averaging across matched demands and visits.
Two-sided sign-flip tests assessed participant-level on-minus-off changes; participant bootstrap resampling provided confidence intervals.
Permutation tests assessed strategy distributions, and paired slope comparisons assessed demand dependence.
Trial-level mixed models adjusted for stimulation state, direction, their interaction, and demand, with participant and nested-visit random intercepts and participant-clustered intervals.
Ward clustering examined standardized behavioral changes, with silhouette scores and omission analyses assessing cluster structure.
Anatomical associations were tested using Spearman correlations with 29,999 permutations and Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
Eligible variables required at least 12 observations and sufficient variation.
Elastic-net models evaluated 42 anatomical predictors using outer leave-one-participant-out prediction and inner fivefold tuning, with preprocessing restricted to training folds.
Prediction errors were compared with the training-cohort mean.
Follow-up models examined associative STN coverage and convergence latency, and fasciculus subthalamicus activation and movement strategy.

text.text: The strongest evidence for an interaction was for final gain (convergence minus divergence, -0.10, p = 0.06).
Interaction p values were 0.96 for first gain, 0.38 for absolute final-gain error, 0.46 for latency, 0.36 for gaze holding, and 0.71 for movement strategy distribution.
To test whether DBS altered the scaling of vergence with stimulus amplitude, we compared off-state and on-state slopes across matched low, intermediate, and high demands within each participant.
Across participants, DBS did not significantly change the demand dependence of final gain, first gain, or latency.

For convergence, the mean slope change was +0.021 gain units/degree for final gain (paired p = 0.32), +0.020 gain units/degree for first gain (paired p = 0.32), and -34 ms/degree for latency (paired p = 0.44).
For divergence, corresponding changes were +0.012 gain units/degree (paired p = 0.41), +0.016 gain units/degree (paired p = 0.21), and +2 ms/degree (paired p = 0.95).
The available data therefore did not establish that DBS altered the demand dependence of gain or latency.
The small average on-off changes in gain, final accuracy, and strategy reflected cancellation among markedly different individual responses.
In several participants, changes in gain magnitude, endpoint accuracy, timing, early accuracy, and movement strategy moved independently, emphasizing that these dimensions should not be conflated.

For example, PD19 showed one of the clearest beneficial responses: final gain increased by 0.35 during convergence and 0.80 during divergence, while absolute final-gain error decreased by 0.85 and 0.50, respectively, and latency shortened in both directions.

In contrast, PD29 and PD31 became substantially more accurate in both directions despite decreases in convergence gain (-0.73 and -0.65, respectively), consistent with correction of excessive off-state responses.

At the opposite extreme, PD18 showed large increases in final gain (+1.31 during convergence and +1.05 during divergence) but became less accurate, with absolute final-gain error increasing by 0.58 and 0.84.
Thus, increased gain could accompany either improvement or deterioration in endpoint performance, depending on the participant's baseline state.
The initial-angular-error analysis reinforced this point.

DBS-related increases in first movement magnitude did not necessarily imply better early accuracy; rather, the change was beneficial only when it moved the participant closer to the requested amplitude.
The largest convergence improvements in initial angular error were seen in PD17 (-3.65°), PD31 (-2.71°), PD12 (-2.57°), PD47 (-2.18°), and PD41 (-2.14°).
For divergence, the largest improvements were observed in PD30 (-4.38°), PD31 (-2.78°), PD19 (-2.44°), PD12 (-1.54°), and PD13 (-1.16°).

However, some participants worsened despite the overall convergence effect, including PD42 for convergence (+1.21°), PD22 (+0.78°), and PD24 (+0.29°), and PD47 for divergence (+1.38°), PD10 (+0.94°), and PD11 (+0.76°).
Other dissociations were also evident.

PD10 and PD28 showed marked shortening of convergence latency (approximately 580 ms and 490 ms, respectively), yet divergence endpoint accuracy worsened by 0.32 and 0.44, indicating that faster initiation and better endpoint accuracy were separable.

PD12 and PD30 showed large increases in first divergence gain (+0.64 and +0.75) with much smaller and opposite-signed changes in final divergence accuracy (+0.16 and -0.10), suggesting that DBS altered the initial motor response more than the eventual endpoint.
Meanwhile, PD17, PD32, and PD41 showed pronounced shifts toward more negative holding in both directions, particularly during convergence, accompanied by some improvement in final accuracy.
Given the marked individual heterogeneity, we asked whether participants could be partitioned into response subgroups.

Hierarchical clustering was performed in all participants with complete profiles using eight standardized features: on-off changes in final-gain error, first gain, latency, and holding, each measured for convergence and divergence.
A small subgroup consisting of PD29 and PD31 emerged consistently.
In the best-performing twocluster solution, these two participants separated from the remaining with a silhouette value of 0.33, reflecting modest but detectable structure.

Both showed large reductions in final-gain error in both directions together with lower first convergence gain, suggesting a similar pattern of DBS-related correction of excessive OFF-state responses.

A three-cluster solution additionally identified a possible gaze holding-shift group (PD17, PD24, PD32, PD41, PD48), but separation was weak (silhouette 0.15), and a four-cluster solution mainly isolated PD10 because of marked divergencelatency change (silhouette 0.18).
Cluster assignments remained reasonably stable when one participant was removed, but were only moderately robust to omission of individual features (median adjusted Rand index 0.55).
The heterogeneous effects of STN DBS on vergence may reflect differential engagement of neural circuits governing distinct aspects of binocular motor control.

Variability in stimulation location, volume of tissue activated, and recruitment of specific white matter pathways may selectively influence vergence initiation, execution, accuracy, gaze holding, and saccade-assisted strategies.
This anatomical variability provides an opportunity to investigate the circuit-level mechanisms underlying these behaviors.

The 42 candidate predictors included hemisphere-specific fiber activation, regional stimulation coverage, and left and right VTA.

Anatomical models reduced squared prediction error by 26.7-35.0% relative to the benchmark, although the advantage diminished substantially after influential participants were excluded.

Under the original strategy classification, greater right sensorimotor STN coverage predicted more frequent use of the vergence-plus-saccade category, whereas greater left associative STN coverage, left fasciculus subthalamicus activation, and right internal capsule coverage each predicted less frequent use.
All four predictors were selected in 18 of 19 training sets, with modest improvement in prediction for held-out participants.

Root mean squared error (RMSE) was 15.3 percentage points with the pathways included, compared with 25.3 for volumes alone and 22.2 for the training-mean benchmark.
This advantage persisted when influential participants were excluded one at a time, suggesting that pathway engagement added predictive information beyond stimulation volume within this cohort.
Because strategy proportions sum to 100%, a decrease in one category corresponds to an increase in one or more others.

The cumulative score summed the bilateral averages for Field of Forel coverage, cerebellothalamic pathway activation.

The specific rationale for choosing these pathways was that its coverage with VTA would retrogradely modulate the cerebellar outflow, influencing the fidelity of vergence neural integrator, affecting gaze holding in convergence or divergence state.

All 19 participants had some modeled Field of Forel coverage on at least one side.
Across participants, the correlation between the cumulative score and the magnitude of change in holding variance was weak (Spearman ρ = -0.23, p = 0.351).
Thus, participants with improved holding had higher median cumulative exposure, but the group difference was statistically inconclusive.

Of the 24 participants in the paired DBS vergence cohort, 19 had imaging and paired motor scores, 14 had paired RAF ruler measurements, and 17 had paired distance-to-pen measurements.
Clinical changes were calculated as DBS on-minus-off.
Negative changes indicate lower motor scores or shorter convergence distances with stimulation.
Associations with modeled fiber activation, regional overlap of the VTA, and overall VTA volume were evaluated using Spearman rank correlations and two-sided permutation tests.
Greater right cerebellothalamic activation was associated with a larger reduction in motor score with DBS on (ρ = -0.52, unadjusted p = 0.025).
The right reticular tract measure yielded the same rank correlation.
Greater left ventro-oralis posterior overlap was associated with a smaller reduction or an increase in motor score (ρ = +0.56, p = 0.014).

After adjustment for off-state motor score and total VTA volume, the partial rank correlations were -0.35 for right cerebellothalamic pathway activation and +0.49 for left ventro-oralis posterior overlap.
Overall VTA volumes showed little association with motor score change (|ρ| ≤ 0.11, all p ≥ 0.662).
Greater right frontal corticopontine tract activation was associated with a longer RAF ruler distance (ρ = +0.55, unadjusted p = .045).
After adjustment for OFF-state RAF ruler distance and total VTA volume, the partial rank correlations were +0.62 and +0.43, respectively.
Overall VTA volumes showed weak associations with RAF ruler distance change (|ρ| ≤ 0.19, all p ≥ .501).

For distance to pen, greater overlap with the right substantia nigra region, defined by the combined pars compacta/pars reticulata atlas label, accompanied a larger shortening with DBS ON (ρ = -0.66, unadjusted p = 0.0050).
Greater activation of the left corticospinal tract (ρ = -0.55, p = .025) and left cerebellothalamic pathway (ρ = -0.53, p = 0.033) also accompanied shorter distances.
After adjustment for OFF-state distance to pen and total VTA volume, the corresponding partial rank correlations were -0.67, -0.60, and -0.57.
Among the overall volume measures, left VTA volume showed the largest correlation with distance to pen (ρ = -0.43, p = 0.090).
Changing viewing depth requires the brain to establish a new binocular alignment and sustain it after the movement ends.
Our findings suggest that STN-region DBS can affect these components differently.
Its clearest effect was on post-vergence gaze stability: eye-position variance decreased by approximately one-third across convergence and divergence.
The initial convergence response also landed closer to the target, whereas average changes in signed gain, final accuracy, latency, and movement strategy were less consistent.
This pattern suggests that a subcortical perturbation can improve the maintenance of binocular alignment with relatively little average change in how the eyes attain it.
Exploratory anatomical analyses identified candidate contributions from associative STN territories and the fields of Forel with adjacent cerebellothalamic projections.

These observations raise the possibility that stimulation influences movement preparation and saccade-vergence coordination through basal ganglia circuits, while modulation of cerebellar signals reaching midbrain vergence circuitry helps stabilize the attained eye position.
The reduction in post-vergence variability provides the strongest behavioral basis for examining this proposed distinction.
STN-region DBS reduced vergence holding variance after both convergence and divergence, with little evidence of a change in final gain.
This finding is consistent with improved fidelity of vergence integration.
Once the eyes reached a new vergence angle, they fluctuated less around it, even though the average achieved angle changed little.
Participants whose gaze holding improved had greater cumulative modeled coverage of the fields of Forel and cerebellothalamic fibers than those whose gaze holding was unchanged.

Together, these observations support the hypothesis that retrograde modulation of cerebellar outflow by engaging field of Forel and cerebellothalamic projections would improve the fidelity of vergence integration, expressed behaviorally as a steadier gaze holding after the vergence movement ends.
One possibility is that stimulation of cerebellothalamic axons alters the cerebellar signals that tune midbrain vergence circuitry.

Field of Forel and cerebellothalamic track modulation can antidromically modulate deep cerebellar nuclei (Tolbert et al., 1978), and modulation of the fastigial and posterior interposed outputs reach the SOA and adjacent central mesencephalic reticular formation (Bohlen et al., 2021).

text.text: The strongest anatomical signal for those individual differences was reduced use of combined responses during divergence with greater left Field of Forel overlap.
Left ventro-oralis anterior overlap and left fasciculus subthalamicus recruitment showed associations in the same direction.
The proximity of pallidothalamic and cerebellothalamic fibers in this region makes Field of Forel overlap a marker of exposure to the border region (Gallay et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The proximity of pallidothalamic and cerebellothalamic fibers in this region makes Field of Forel overlap a marker of exposure to the border region <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gallay et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: It leaves open contributions from pallidothalamic output, pallidal-subthalamic interactions, and adjacent cerebellothalamic fibers.

The modeled stimulation overlap with the campi Foreli, pallidothalamic projections, and cerebellothalamic projections suggest a complementary route to modulate saccade vergence collaboration to achieve gaze shift in depth.
Within this anatomy, pallidal output could bias the anticipated movement strategy, including whether a smooth response is likely to suffice and when a saccade should be released if it is recruited.

Cerebellar output could calibrate the selected response, including how much of the remaining vergence error the saccade should remove and how the eyes settle afterward (Busettini and Mays, 2005 , Ilinsky et al., 2018 , Sakai et al., 1996 , Takeichi et al., 2005).

text.text: Cerebellar output, caudal fastigial and posterior interposed nuclei project to distinct parts of the midbrain cMRF (Bohlen et al., 2021 , May et al., 1990 , May et al., 1992); the region relevant to saccades.

text.text: Saccade-vergence burst neurons in this region discharge in relation to vergence velocity; the rapid vergence contribution depends on the interaction of a saccadic burst with the vergence error remaining when the saccade begins (Busettini and Mays, 2005, Quinet et al., 2020).

text.text: In this way STN DBS, via recruiting and antidromically modulating cerebellothalamic projection can modulate when the saccadic burst arrives relative to the evolving vergence error, how strongly the burst contributes to the change in binocular alignment (Gallay et al., 2008 , McIntyre et al., 2004).

text.text: Binocular near viewing depends on how the brain uses visual cues to align and focus the eyes and then keep them steady.
Our findings suggest that STN DBS may influence different parts of this process.
Video-oculography showed steadier gaze after a depth shift, with greater combined stimulation coverage of the field of Forel and adjacent cerebellothalamic pathways among participants who improved.
The bedside tests probed how well binocular alignment or single vision was maintained as disparity, blur, and proximity cues changed together.

Greater left cerebellothalamic activation was associated with a closer pen-tip breakpoint, whereas greater right frontal corticopontine activation and internal capsule overlap were associated with a more distant RAF ruler breakpoint.

These exploratory findings raise the possibility that cerebellar outflow helps stabilize an attained vergence position, while frontal signals relayed through the pons and cerebellum may shape how visual cues drive the midbrain near response (Bohlen et al., 2021 , Gallay et al., 2008 , Gamlin and Clarke, 1995 , Gamlin and Yoon, 2000 , Horwood and Riddell, 2009 , Zhang and Gamlin, 1998).

A prospective within-participant study pairing targeted stimulation with eye tracking, bedside testing, and reading measures could determine whether steadier gaze also helps patients with Parkinson's disease maintain single vision as viewing demands change.   exposure.
